definition: Veracity means truthfulness; conformity to fact.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word veracity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know veracity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The hiring manager doubted the veracity of a resume listing 'fluent in eleven languages' beside a misspelled hometown.
Sincerity means you believe what you say; veracity sets the higher bar—what you say must also match the facts.
Infallibility towers over veracity: a witness of perfect veracity tells the truth as the facts show it, while an infallible one could never be wrong at all—a standard no witness meets.

Truthfulness is the everyday virtue of telling the truth, and it lives in a person's intentions. Veracity is the formal, testable version that courts and editors invoke: whether an account actually matches the facts once checked. A truthful narrator means every word; veracity asks whether the entries hold up.

Accuracy is correctness of detail, and it needs no one behind it — a map can be accurate, and so can a guess. Veracity belongs to tellers and their accounts: it is truthfulness measured against fact, so it can be doubted only where someone is making a claim.

Veracity is narrower than 'honesty': honesty is a person's overall virtue, while veracity is the truth-to-fact quality of statements and accounts.
A kind, honest man can still write a log with poor veracity if his memory embroiders.

In 1936, a climber named Edda Voss returned from the Karakoram claiming a solo first ascent of a peak called the White Horn.
Reporters loved her; rival climbers did not, and they questioned the veracity of her account in every alpine journal that would print them.
She handed the editors her negatives, her barometric log, and the torn page of a tea-house register from the far side of the pass.
A panel spent two winters checking: the shadows in the photographs matched the date, the pressure readings matched the altitude, the register matched the route.
What her rivals had treated as a story to doubt turned out to be an account that agreed, point by point, with the facts.
